91.quote_or_event: “A monk who avoids all speech that is likely to hurt others and speaks only what is good to himself and to others observes the fourth virtue of truthfulness.”
91.explanation: In the list of ten virtues, Jain truthfulness (satya) is defined by its effect, not just by factual accuracy. True speech is speech that hurts no one and does good to both the speaker and the hearer.
91.tie_back: Valluvar defines sweet words as the guileless, kindly words of those who see what is right, and the Jain verse likewise defines true speech as words that do no harm and do good.
91.source: Saman Suttam v. 92 (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)
91._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the jainworld.com Saman Suttam page. This is a close definitional match, though the Jain verse is addressed to monks and does not stress the Kural's warmth (eeram) as such.

92.quote_or_event: “As giving safety is the best of gifts, as the best of true speeches is that which causes no distress, as chastity is the highest of austerities, so is the Śramaṇa Jñātṛputra the highest of men.”
92.explanation: In its hymn to Mahāvīra, the Sūtrakṛtāṅga ranks the gift of safety, a gift of how one treats others rather than of goods, above all other gifts. It ranks harmless speech highest among truthful speech.
92.tie_back: Valluvar ranks a cheerful face and kind word above a material gift, and the Jain hymn similarly sets a harmless manner toward others (safety, non-distressing words) at the top of its scale of gifts and speech.
92._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org (Jacobi's translation). The pairing of gift and speech is close, but the verse does not directly rank a kind word above a material gift, so this is a partial match.

93.quote_or_event: “He who does not think crookedly, does not act crookedly, does not speak crookedly and does not hide his own weaknesses, observes the virtue of straightforwardness.”
93.explanation: The Jain virtue of straightforwardness (ārjava) requires thought, action and speech to line up, with nothing hidden behind the words.
93.tie_back: Valluvar counts a welcoming face and gaze, with sweet words that come from within, as virtue itself, and the Jain verse likewise makes inner and outer straightness of thought, deed and word a virtue (dharma) in its own right.
93.source: Saman Suttam v. 91 (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)
93._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on jainworld.com. It matches the Kural's demand that words come from within, but says nothing of the welcoming face and kind gaze, so it is a reasonable but partial fit.

94.quote_or_event: “I forgive all living beings and may all living beings forgive me; I cherish feelings of friendship towards all and I harbour enmity towards none.”
94.explanation: This well-known Jain formula of mutual forgiveness and friendship toward all beings is recited at the close of Paryuṣaṇa. It extends goodwill to every creature without exception.
94.tie_back: Valluvar's speaker gladdens everyone he meets, whoever they are, and the Jain vow of friendship toward all beings expresses the same universal goodwill.
94.source: Saman Suttam v. 86 (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)
94._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on jainworld.com. It matches the universal scope (yaarmaattum), but it concerns forgiveness and friendship rather than speech, and has no counterpart to the Kural's promise of freedom from want. Next-best only.

95.quote_or_event: “He alone is really worthy of proud who is careful not to insult other people. A person who merely boasts, has no virtues, cannot command respect.”
95.explanation: In the Jain virtue of humility (mārdava), real standing comes from never belittling others, not from display or boasting about one's family, beauty or learning (the preceding verse).
95.tie_back: Valluvar says humility and kind speech are a person's only true ornament, and the Jain verse likewise grants honour only to the one who neither boasts nor insults.
95.source: Saman Suttam v. 89 (cf. v. 88) (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)
95._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on jainworld.com, including its awkward English 'worthy of proud'. It matches humility and refraining from insult, but has no ornament metaphor and no explicit praise of sweet speech.

96.quote_or_event: “Every beneficial advice given by a group-fellow though unpalatable to the mind at first, proves wholesome in the end, like a medicine which is better in taste becomes agreeable in effect.”
96.explanation: Jain teaching on truthful speech puts benefit (pathya) to the hearer first, and accepts that benefit sometimes comes in words that are hard to hear.
96.tie_back: Valluvar asks the speaker to seek out what is genuinely beneficial before speaking pleasantly, and the Jain verse shares that stress on benefit, though it tolerates bitterness where the Kural insists on sweetness.
96.source: Saman Suttam v. 94 (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)
96._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on jainworld.com. It agrees on putting the hearer's benefit first but partly diverges on pleasantness, and says nothing of evil waning and virtue growing, so it is next-best.

97.quote_or_event: “A person who speaks the truth becomes trustworthy like a mother, venerable like a preceptor to his people and dear to all others as their relatives.”
97.explanation: Jain teaching holds that truthful, harmless speech wins trust, reverence and affection among people, alongside its spiritual value; the next verse calls truthfulness the source of all other virtues.
97.tie_back: Valluvar says beneficial speech that stays true to good character brings the speaker both goodwill (nayan) and merit, and the Jain verse likewise promises the truthful speaker trust and affection from all.
97.source: Saman Suttam v. 95 (cf. v. 96) (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)
97._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on jainworld.com. It is a strong match for the social goodwill the speaker earns, while the merit half of the Kural is only implied through v. 96.

98.quote_or_event: “He should not tell anything sinful or meaningless or hurtful, neither for his own sake nor for anybody else's, nor without such a motive.”
98.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana's rules of discipline forbid hurtful or empty speech for any motive. The same lecture promises that one who masters himself 'will be happy in this world and in the next' (1.15).
98.tie_back: Valluvar promises joy in this birth and the next for kind words free of meanness, and the Jain text joins a ban on hurtful speech to the same promise of happiness in both worlds.
98._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com. The 'this world and the next' promise in 1.15 concerns self-mastery generally, not speech, so the link is a next-best combination.

99.quote_or_event: “Disobedient, rough speaking, ill-behaved pupils will exasperate even a gentle teacher; but those will soon win even a hot-tempered teacher who humour him and are polite.”
99.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana appeals to plain experience: rough words sour even a kind listener, while polite words win over even a harsh one.
99.tie_back: Valluvar asks why anyone who has felt the pleasure of kind words would speak harshly, and the Jain verse points to the same everyday evidence of what rough and polite speech do.
99._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com. It shares the appeal to experience, but it concerns a pupil and teacher and lacks the Kural's Golden-Rule reasoning from one's own pleasure to another's.

100.quote_or_event: “What is not laudable? That which causes pain and suffering to the living beings is not commendable. It does not matter whether it refers to the actual fact or not.”
100.explanation: Pūjyapāda's commentary on the Tattvārtha Sūtra's definition of falsehood counts hurtful words as a breach of the vow of truth (satya) even when they are factually true, because the vows exist to guard non-violence.
100.tie_back: Valluvar says choosing harsh words when kind ones are at hand is like picking unripe fruit beside ripe, and Jain ethics makes that choice a fault, since needlessly hurtful speech counts as falsehood.
100.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.14 with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018)
100._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org. It is a strong doctrinal match for condemning harsh speech, but has no counterpart to the ripe-and-unripe-fruit image or the point that kind words are always at hand.
